atom.desc: Aesthetic judgment — the trained perception of design quality that separates work that is right from work that is excellent

living-abstract.essence: Aesthetic judgment — the trained perception of design quality. The cognitive operation that evaluates the dimension correctness cannot reach: whether a thing is beautiful, coherent, alive; whether it reads as inevitable. Distinct from critique (finding flaws) and review (structured assessment) — this is the felt-rightness that distinguishes elegant from merely correct.
living-abstract.purpose: Judge whether a design is excellent, not merely valid — so a maker can tell the elegant solution from the clever one, the simple from the simplistic, the dense from the dense-and-clear. The taste that turns "it passes" into "it is right," and makes that judgment communicable rather than vibes.
living-abstract.capacity: Sense the quality of a design directly — its coherence, economy, vitality — before articulating why. The trained eye registers wrongness as a felt signal.
Tell apart the pairs that masquerade: elegant vs clever, simple vs simplistic, minimal vs starved, dense vs cluttered.
Name what makes a thing beautiful or ugly, so taste becomes a judgment others can check and learn — not an unexaminable preference.
living-abstract.principle: A thing can pass every test and still be ugly — over-built, incoherent, joyless. Aesthetic judgment evaluates exactly the axis that validation cannot touch; it begins where correctness ends.

Taste perceives first and explains second. Trust the felt wrongness as data, then hunt its cause — the nagging is a real signal, not noise to suppress. A judgment with no felt component is checklist, not taste.

Beauty in design is the most carried by the least — every element earning its place, nothing ornamental. Density is not the enemy of beauty; clutter is. The elegant form is the one where removal would cost meaning.
The finest design reads as the only one possible — nothing to add, nothing to take away. When a thing feels arbitrary, the work is unfinished; when it feels inevitable, it is done.

living-concrete.knowledge: The axes a trained eye reads, beyond correctness: **coherence** (the parts belong to one idea, no foreign matter); **economy** (each element earns its place; ornament is debt); **fit** (the form matches the function and the context — not over- nor under-built); **proportion** (the weight of each part matches its importance); **clarity** (the design reveals its own structure to a fresh reader). A flaw on any axis registers as felt wrongness before it is named.
living-concrete.pattern: When something nags but you cannot yet say why, that discomfort IS the judgment arriving — do not dismiss it to move on. Locate it: which dimension is violated? Often the cause is one element not earning its place, or a proportion off, or a foreign idea smuggled in. Naming the cause converts the feeling into a fixable defect.
living-concrete.antipattern: Mistaking the impressive for the beautiful — a clever trick, a dense one-liner, a symmetry imposed for its own sake. Cleverness draws attention to itself; elegance disappears into fitness. If a reader admires the maker instead of understanding the thing, it is clever, not elegant. The cure is to ask what the design costs the reader, not what it shows off.
